opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the first thing to say is that it's not so much skepticism as a different way of thinking about what these systems are. The way I like to put it is that large language models are cultural technologies, not intelligent agents. They're more like the printing press, or libraries, or the internet itself. They're incredibly good at summarizing and passing on information that other people, other humans, have already figured out. That's a real and important kind of intelligence. Cultural transmission is one of the things that makes human beings so special.

But that's very different from what a two-year-old is doing. If you watch a two-year-old, they're out there in the world doing experiments all the time. We call it "getting into everything," but from a scientist's perspective, what they're really doing is intervening in the world, seeing what happens, and figuring out the causal structure of the world around them. They're discovering new things, things they couldn't have known just from listening to what other people tell them.

And we've done experiments where we actually compare children and these models. We give them a new problem, say, a machine that lights up when you put certain combinations of blocks on it, or a problem where you have to figure out a new use for an everyday object. If you ask, "What goes with a ruler?" the model will say a compass, because those words appear together a lot. But if you ask, "I need to draw a circle and I don't have a compass, what could I use?" a four-year-old will say, "Well, you could use a teapot, because it's round." The child has a model of how the world actually works, and they can use it to solve a genuinely new problem. The language models are much worse at that kind of innovation, because they're drawing on the statistics of what's already been said rather than on going out and exploring.

So the contrast is between imitation and exploration. Both are crucial, and children do both. But the exploratory part, the being in the world, acting on it, being curious about it, and revising what you think in light of what happens, that's something two-year-olds do effortlessly and that we really don't know how to build into these systems yet.

r001.rationale: It says two-year-olds experiment by intervening in the world and learning from outcomes, while language models are worse at this exploratory ability.

r002.rationale: It contrasts models’ reliance on previously stated information with real-world exploration, but does not connect text generation without external contact to postmodernism or the idea that text alone is sufficient.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the first thing I'd say is that I think "skeptical" isn't quite the right frame. I'm not skeptical that these systems are impressive, or that they're doing something interesting. What I'm skeptical of is the idea that what they're doing is the same kind of thing that a two-year-old is doing, and that's partly because I think we've been asking the wrong question about them. We keep asking, "Are they intelligent? Are they agents?" and I think the better way to think about them is as cultural technologies, more like writing or printing or libraries or the internet. They're extraordinarily good at taking the vast amount of stuff that humans have already produced and summarizing it, recombining it, making it accessible. That's genuinely valuable. But it's a different thing from going out into the world and finding out something new.

And that's what two-year-olds do. The thing that strikes you if you actually watch a two-year-old, which, to be fair, most people who build these systems haven't spent a lot of time doing, is that they're constantly getting information from the world directly. They're picking things up, dropping them, putting them in their mouths, pushing the button again and again. From the outside it looks like chaos, but what they're really doing is running little experiments. They have a model of how the world works, they act on it, the world pushes back, and they revise the model. That loop, acting in the world and getting feedback from the world, is what lets them solve problems they've never seen before. A language model has nothing like that. It's learning from text that other people produced, which is a kind of secondhand evidence about the world rather than the world itself.

The other piece is what we'd call truth-tracking. A child's learning system is built so that what it believes is constrained by what's actually out there. If the block doesn't balance, it doesn't balance, no matter what anybody says. The language models are trained to predict what people are likely to say next, and what people say is only loosely connected to what's true. That's why you get these very fluent, very plausible outputs that happen to be wrong. It's not a bug you can patch, it's a consequence of the objective.

And then there's the sheer amount of data. These systems need something like trillions of words. A child by age three has heard maybe a few million, and they still manage to figure out causal structure, other people's intentions, how objects behave, all of it. So whatever children are doing, it's not just a scaled-down version of what the models are doing. It's a different algorithm, and I'd say it's the more interesting one. If we really understood it, that would be a scientific achievement on the order of understanding how evolution works, and I don't think we're there yet.

r001.rationale: It describes two-year-olds running experiments by acting on the world and getting feedback, and says language models lack that loop.

r002.rationale: It contrasts learning from text with learning from the world, but does not connect this to postmodernism or the idea that text alone is sufficient.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think the striking thing about two-year-olds is that they don’t just learn from information that somebody else has already collected. They go out and get new information. They intervene in the world. They try something, see what happens, and then try something else. And often what looks to us like a child being a nuisance—dropping the spoon off the high chair for the twentieth time—is actually a very effective way of finding out how the world works.

Large language models are extraordinarily good at extracting patterns from the language that humans have produced. But that’s a different task from discovering something that you don’t already know by acting on the world. If you’re faced with a new problem, you need to figure out which experiment to do, what evidence would distinguish one explanation from another, and how to change your mind when things don’t work.

Now, that isn’t to say that an artificial system couldn’t do those things. But being very good at predicting what a person would say isn’t, by itself, evidence that you can learn the way a two-year-old does. The interesting question is what else you would need to add.

r001.rationale: The response says two-year-olds intervene in the world, try things, observe outcomes, and experiment to learn, while distinguishing this from LLMs’ pattern extraction from human language.

r002.rationale: It contrasts language-pattern extraction with acting on the world, but does not connect LLM text generation without external contact to the postmodernist idea that text alone is sufficient.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I think the important distinction is between learning from what other people have said about the world and learning by actually doing things in the world. Language is an extraordinarily powerful way of transmitting knowledge. But a two-year-old can encounter something she’s never seen before, poke it, try something else, and work out how it operates. She’s intervening in the world and using the results to figure out its causal structure.

And she’s not just trying to accomplish a task that someone has specified. She’s making up new problems. What happens if I put this thing inside that thing? What happens if I do it again? That apparently aimless exploration is doing an enormous amount of work.

Large language models are remarkably good at extracting patterns from the accumulated products of human thought. What’s less clear is whether that gives them the capacity to discover something genuinely new through that kind of open-ended exploration. They can describe what a curious child does very convincingly. But describing the process and actually being able to carry it out are different achievements.

r001.rationale: The response says a two-year-old can poke an unfamiliar object, try things, and use the results to learn how it works, while questioning whether language models can discover through that exploration.

r002.rationale: The response contrasts learning from language with acting in the world, but does not connect language models’ text generation to postmodernism or the idea that text alone is sufficient.
